summary: A 1975 proposal that extends the message field definitions begun in RFC 561, in an effort to set syntactic and semantic standards for ARPANET messages. It sits in the line of work that led to RFC 733 and RFC 822.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 680 defines additional fields for network messages, including fields for recipients, references and handling. It aims to make the fields understandable to people and usable by programs.

subtitle: A proposed set of message fields extending the format in RFC 561.

tldr.problem: Sites needed common syntax and meanings for message fields beyond those described in RFC 561.
tldr.mechanism: The document restates the basic message format and defines fields for senders, recipients, references and message handling.
tldr.outcome: The format remains compatible with RFC 561, but the RFC expects that not every message server will process every field.

today: RFC 680 has status listed as Unknown and updates RFC 561. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 680.

sections.title: Goal and Approach
sections.content:
RFC 680 defines fields beyond those discussed in RFC 561. It keeps the overall message format compatible with RFC 561 and sets out proposed syntax and meanings for the additional fields.

The authors do not expect every message server to process every field automatically. They use angle brackets around some machine-readable notations to make them easier for automatic processes to recognize, while keeping the specification general enough for experimentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives shared names and meanings to more message labels. Some labels are for programs to process, while others can still help people reading a message.

sections.title: Basic Message Structure
sections.content:
A message contains a header, a carriage-return/line-feed separator and a body. The required header items are DATE and SENDER. Optional items include SUBJECT, Message-ID, TO, CC, BCC and fields such as FROM, IN-REPLY-TO, REFERENCES, KEYWORD, PRECEDENCE and MESSAGE-CLASS.

A message can contain at most one MESSAGE-ID item. The case of keywords is not significant. The sender field names a user at a host, and the date includes a time and zone.
sections.plainLanguage: A message has a labeled header followed by its text. DATE and SENDER are required; many other labels can be added when useful.

sections.title: People, References and Recipients
sections.content:
FROM identifies the person who wanted the message sent. SENDER identifies the person who sends it and is expected to be set by the message-creation process. AUTHENTICATION describes which originator fields have been authenticated and by which operating systems.

MESSAGE-ID is a unique identifier based on a network address and text. IN-REPLY-TO and REFERENCES identify earlier correspondence. TO names primary recipients, CC secondary recipients and BCC tertiary recipients; BCC should not be shown to primary or secondary recipients, though it may be recorded for access control.
sections.plainLanguage: FROM names who wanted the message sent, and SENDER names who sent it. TO, CC and BCC identify recipient groups, with BCC hidden from the first two groups.

sections.title: Message-Type and Handling Fields
sections.content:
PRECEDENCE describes importance and urgency. The notation <PRIORITY> means the message should be delivered as soon as possible; <ROUTINE> means priority processing is not needed. MESSAGE-CLASS describes the message's legal status, with examples including Official, Unofficial, Record and Off the Record.

SPECIAL-HANDLING gives instructions for the receiving end. The notation <PRIVATE> means the receiving process should not help the user circulate copies. Plain text may also appear in these fields.
sections.plainLanguage: These fields can describe how urgent a message is, its stated class and any special handling requested. The memo does not expect automatic processing of every field.

references.text: RFC 561, the base message format extended by RFC 680.
